newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Confusion over Germans jailed in Colombian kidnap.
newsitem.headline: Confusion over Germans jailed in Colombian kidnap.

text.p: There were confusing accounts on Monday as to whether two Germans -- arrested over the weekend trying to smuggle a kidnap victim out of the country -- were themselves victims or villains of Colombia's booming kidnap trade.

The two, apparently husband and wife, were seized at the Rionegro airport outside the northwest city of Medellin before dawn on Sunday as they tried to bundle a third German, Brigitte Schoene, onto a charter flight for Venezuela.

Schoene, wife of a former BASF Chemicals executive, had been held since Aug. 15 by leftist National Liberation Army (ELN) guerrillas who abducted her at her Rionegro home and demanded up to $6 million for her release.

Gen. Alfredo Salgado, head of the anti-kidnapping police in Antioquia, the northwest province of which Medellin is the capital, told reporters on Sunday that the two Germans arrested were believed to part of the ELN's international financial structure.
At a news conference on Monday, Salgado added that the man, who is missing the tip of his left index finger, had been identified through checks with Interpol as Werner Mauss.
German news reports said Mauss was a former state security agent who now worked as an adviser to leading German companies.

The German embassy in Bogota has declined to comment on the arrests, but some officials said Mauss and his companion may simply have been acting as intermediaries to secure Schoene's release from her rebel captors in exchange for a ransom.

The only formal charges filed against the Germans so far stems from the fact that both were found to be carrying false identity papers when they were detained at Rionegro's Jose Maria Cordoba international airport.

Schoene, who put in a brief appearance at Monday's news conference, looked surprisingly fit, considering the fact that she said she had been confined to a mosquito-infested hole in the Antioquia jungle for most of the past three months.
She said she had never before met the Germans who intervened, innocently or in cahoots with the ELN, to end her ordeal.

Colombia has the world's highest kidnapping rate, with an average of about one person abducted every 2-1/2 hours. About half the kidnappings are attributed by security experts to rebels seeking to raise money for their long-running war against the state.
The ELN, Colombia's second largest guerrilla group, was founded by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966. It specializes in kidnappings and a nationwide campaign of economic sabotage.
